topic.name: Radius of Convergence of Power Series

question.text: Find the radius of convergence $R$ for the series \[ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{3^n}{n+2}\,\left(x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^n=\dfrac{1}{2}+\left(x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+\dfrac{3^2}{4}\,\left(x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2+\dfrac{3^3}{5}\,\left(x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3+\cdots \,. \]
question.explanation:
To apply the ratio test we define $a_n=\dfrac{3^n}{n+2}\,\left(x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^n.$Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to\infty\mathbin{:}$

\[ \begin{align*} L&=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| \\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\dfrac{3^{n+1}\left(x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n+1}}{n+3}\cdot\dfrac{n+2}{3^{n}\left(x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{n}}\right|\\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\dfrac{3(n+2)}{n+3}\left(x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)\right|\\[5pt] &=\left|x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right|\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\dfrac{3(n+2)}{n+3}\\[5pt] &=\left|x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right|\cdot 3 \\[5pt] &= 3 \left|x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right| \end{align*} \]

The series converges if $L< 1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied if $\left|x+\dfrac{1}{4}\right|< \dfrac{1}{3}.$ Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\dfrac{1}{3}.$

example.title: Finding the Radius and Interval of Convergence of a Power Series

question.text:
Given that the power series $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n (x-1)^n$ converges at $x = -3,$ which of the following must be true?

  1. The series converges at $x = 5$
  2. The series diverges at $x=-4$
  3. The series converges at $x=-2$
question.explanation:
The center of the expansion is $x = 1,$ and since the series is convergent for $x = -3,$ this means that the radius of convergence $R$ is at least $4,$ i.e., $R \geq 4.$ So, the series is convergent for every point in the interval $[-3,5).$ However, we know nothing about the convergence of the series at any point outside the interval $[-3,5).$

With this in mind, let's check each of our statements.

  • Statement I is false. Since $5 \notin [-3,5),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is convergent at $x=5.$

  • Statement II is false. Since $-4 \notin [-3,5),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is divergent at $x=-4.$

  • Statement III is true. Since $-2 \in [-3,5),$ the series is convergent at $x=-2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

example.title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Convergence of a Power Series

question.text:
Given that the power series $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n (x+7)^n$ converges at $x=-3,$ which of the following must be true?

  1. The series converges at $x=-11$
  2. The series converges at $x=-8$
  3. The series converges at $x=1$
question.explanation:
The center of the expansion is $x=-7,$ and since the series is convergent for $x=-3,$ this means that the radius of convergence $R$ is at least $4,$ i.e., $R \geq 4 .$ So, the series is convergent for every point in the interval $(-11,-3].$ However, we know nothing about the convergence of the series at any point outside the interval $(-11,-3].$

With this in mind, let's check each of our statements.

  • Statement I is false. Since $-11\notin (-11,-3],$ we cannot guarantee that the series is convergent at $x=-11.$

  • Statement II is true. Since $-8\in (-11,-3],$ the series is convergent at $x=-8.$

  • Statement III is false. Since $1\notin (-11,-3],$ we cannot guarantee that the series is convergent at $x=1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

example.title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Convergence of a Power Series

question.text:
Find the radius of convergence $R$ for the series
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(x+3)^n}{2^{n^{2}}}=\dfrac{x+3}{2}+\dfrac{(x+3)^2}{2^{4}}+\dfrac{(x+3)^3}{2^{9}}+\cdots \,.
\]
question.explanation:
To apply the ratio test, we define $a_n=\dfrac{(x+3)^n}{2^{n^{2}}}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to\infty\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} L&=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| \\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{\dfrac{(x+3)^{n+1}}{2^{(n+1)^{2}}}}{\dfrac{(x+3)^n}{2^{n^{2}}}}\right|\\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{(x+3)^{n+1}}{2^{(n+1)^{2}}}\cdot\frac{2^{n^{2}}}{(x+3)^n}\right|\\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{x+3}{2^{(n+1)^{2}-n^{2}}}\right|\\[5pt] %&=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{x+3}{2^{2n+1}}\right|\\[5pt] &=|x+3|\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{2^{2n+1}}\\[5pt] &=|x+3|\cdot 0\\[5pt] & = 0 \end{align*}

The series converges if $L< 1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for all $-\infty < x < \infty.$ Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\infty}.$

example.title: Finding the Radius and Interval of Convergence of a Power Series

question.text:
Find the radius of convergence $R$ for the series
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n!}=(x-2)+\dfrac{(x-2)^2}{2!}+\dfrac{(x-2)^3}{3!}+\cdots \,.
\]
question.explanation:
To apply the ratio test, we define $a_n=\dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n!}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to\infty\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} L&=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| \\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{\dfrac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}}{\dfrac{(x-2)^n}{n!}}\right|\\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{(x-2)^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\cdot\frac{n!}{(x-2)^n}\right|\\[5pt] &=|x-2|\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n+1}\\[5pt] &=|x-2|\cdot 0\\[5pt] & = 0 \end{align*}

The series converges if $L< 1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for all $-\infty < x < \infty.$ Therefore, we conclude that the radius of convergence is $R=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\infty}.$
